summary:
Joshua opens where Deuteronomy ends: Moses is dead east of the Jordan, and the LORD commissions his assistant, Joshua son of Nun, to lead Israel into the land promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18–21). The repeated charge is "Be strong and courageous" (1:6, 9, 18). Joshua's Hebrew name, Yehoshua, means "The LORD is salvation"; its Greek form, Iēsous, is the same name rendered "Jesus" in the New Testament. The book falls into halves: conquest (chapters 1–12), then division of the land (13–24).

Priests carrying the ark of the covenant — the gold-covered chest holding the tablets of the law — step into the flooded Jordan and the river stops; the text draws its own parallel, "just as He did to the Red Sea" (4:23). Jericho falls after seven days of marching, horn blasts, and a shout, and everything in it is "devoted to the LORD for destruction" (6:17) — Hebrew cherem, something placed irrevocably beyond human use. Two fates then cut across national lines. Rahab, the Canaanite prostitute who hid Israel's spies, is spared with her family; the New Testament cites her faith (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25), and Matthew's genealogy of Jesus lists a Rahab as Boaz's mother (Matthew 1:5). Achan the Israelite takes some of the devoted things, and Israel is routed at Ai until the theft is exposed (chapter 7). The Gibeonites trick Israel into a treaty — the leaders "did not seek the counsel of the LORD" (9:14) — and Israel keeps the oath anyway. Southern and northern campaigns follow (10–11), including the day at Gibeon when "the sun stood still" (10:13).

Chapters 13–21 divide the land tribe by tribe, boundary by boundary. Caleb, now eighty-five, claims the hill country Moses promised him forty-five years earlier and drives out the Anakim, the giants of the scouts' report (14:10–12; Numbers 13:33). The Levites, Israel's priestly tribe, receive forty-eight cities rather than a territory (21:41). The eastern tribes' large altar by the Jordan nearly sparks war until they explain it is a witness to shared worship, not a rival shrine (chapter 22). The book states two things side by side: "Not one of all the LORD's good promises to the house of Israel had failed" (21:45), yet "very much of the land remains to be possessed" (13:1). Judges 1 opens with that unfinished fight, and interpreters relate the two in different ways.

Joshua closes with two farewell speeches. In chapter 23 he warns that the God who kept every promise will just as surely bring calamity if Israel serves other gods (23:15–16). In chapter 24 he gathers the tribes at Shechem, retells the story from Abraham onward in God's own voice, and puts the choice: "choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve… As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD!" (24:15). Three times the people answer that they will serve the LORD; Joshua makes a covenant and sets up a stone as witness. The book ends with three burials: Joshua at 110, the bones of Joseph carried up from Egypt (Genesis 50:25) and laid at Shechem, and Eleazar the priest (24:29–33).
